claim: Computer programming is a novel cognitive tool that has transformed modern society.
source: Computer programming is a novel cognitive tool that has transformed modern society.
evidence: This is a general statement about the societal impact of programming, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Little is known about the cognitive and neural systems that underlie computer programming skills.
source: The ability to flexibly instruct programmable machines has led to a rapid technological transformation of communities across the world (Ensmenger, 2012); however, little is known about the cognitive and neural systems that underlie computer programming skills.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and represents a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Code comprehension refers to a set of cognitive processes that allow programmers to interpret program tokens, combine them to extract meaning of statements, and combine statements into a mental representation of the entire program.
source: By code comprehension, we refer to a set of cognitive processes that allow programmers to interpret individual program tokens (such as keywords, variables, and function names), combine them to extract the meaning of program statements, and, finally, combine the statements into a mental representation of the entire program.
evidence: This is a definitional claim that establishes the scope of the study.

claim: Code comprehension may be cognitively and neurally separable from cognitive operations required to process program content.
source: It is important to note that code comprehension may be cognitively and neurally separable from cognitive operations required to process program content, that is, the actual operations described by code.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on logical reasoning about different aspects of programming.

claim: Processing program content recruits cognitive processes known as computational thinking, which include algorithm identification, pattern generalization/abstraction, and recursive reasoning.
source: Most of the time, processing program content recruits a range of cognitive processes known as computational thinking (Wing, 2006; Wing, 2011), which include algorithm identification, pattern generalization/abstraction, and recursive reasoning (e.g., Kao, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on computational thinking.

claim: Computational thinking operations may not require programming knowledge at all.
source: These cognitive operations are notably different from code comprehension per se and may not require programming knowledge at all (Guzdial, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Code comprehension is expected to draw on preexisting cognitive systems because it is a novel cognitive tool typically acquired in late childhood or adulthood.
source: Given that code comprehension is a novel cognitive tool, typically acquired in late childhood or in adulthood, we expect it to draw on preexisting cognitive systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of skill acquisition and general principles of cognitive development.

claim: Code comprehension may rely on domain-general executive resources, including working memory and cognitive control.
source: First, it may rely on domain-general executive resources, including working memory and cognitive control (Bergersen and Gustafsson, 2011; Nakagawa et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2003).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Code comprehension may draw on cognitive systems associated with math and logic.
source: In addition, it may draw on the cognitive systems associated with math and logic (McNamara, 1967; Papert, 1972), in line with the traditional construal of coding as problem-solving (Dalbey and Linn, 1985; Ormerod, 1990; Pea and Kurland, 1984; Pennington and Grabowski, 1990).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior research on programming and problem-solving.

claim: Code comprehension may rely on the system that supports comprehension of natural languages.
source: Finally, code comprehension may rely on the system that supports comprehension of natural languages (Fedorenko et al., 2019; Murnane, 1993; Papert, 1993).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Computer code makes heavy use of hierarchical structures, similar to natural language.
source: Like natural language, computer code makes heavy use of hierarchical structures (e.g., loops, conditionals, and recursive statements), and, like language, it can convey an unlimited amount of meaningful information (e.g., describing objects or action sequences).
evidence: This is a claim about structural similarities between code and language, based on established knowledge about both domains.

claim: Computer code can convey an unlimited amount of meaningful information, like natural language.
source: Like natural language, computer code makes heavy use of hierarchical structures (e.g., loops, conditionals, and recursive statements), and, like language, it can convey an unlimited amount of meaningful information (e.g., describing objects or action sequences).
evidence: This is a claim about the expressive capacity of code, based on established knowledge.

claim: Executive processes recruit a set of bilateral frontal and parietal brain regions collectively known as the multiple demand (MD) system.
source: Prior research (Assem et al., 2020; Duncan, 2010; Duncan, 2013; Duncan and Owen, 2000) has shown that executive processes – such as attention, working memory, and cognitive control – recruit a set of bilateral frontal and parietal brain regions collectively known as the multiple demand (MD) system.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging research.

claim: If code comprehension primarily relies on domain-general executive processes, code-evoked responses should be observed within the MD system, distributed across both hemispheres.
source: If code comprehension primarily relies on domain-general executive processes, we expect to observe code-evoked responses within the MD system, distributed across both hemispheres.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about the MD system and logical inference.

claim: Math and logic evoke responses within the MD system, and this activity tends to be left-lateralized.
source: Math and logic also evoke responses within the MD system (Fedorenko et al., 2013), although this activity tends to be left-lateralized (Amalric and Dehaene, 2016; Amalric and Dehaene, 2019; Goel and Dolan, 2001; Micheloyannis et al., 2005; Monti et al., 2007; Monti et al., 2009; Pinel and Dehaene, 2010; Prabhakaran et al., 1997; Reverberi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior neuroimaging research.

claim: If code comprehension draws on the same mechanisms as math and logic, left-lateralized activity within the MD system should be observed.
source: If code comprehension draws on the same mechanisms as math and logic, we expect to observe left-lateralized activity within the MD system.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about math/logic processing and logical inference.

claim: Comprehension of natural language recruits a set of left frontal and temporal brain regions known as the language system.
source: Finally, comprehension of natural language recruits a set of left frontal and temporal brain regions known as the language system (e.g., Fedorenko and Thompson-Schill, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Language regions respond robustly to linguistic input, both visual and auditory.
source: These regions respond robustly to linguistic input, both visual and auditory (Deniz et al., 2019; Fedorenko et al., 2010; Nakai et al., 2020; Regev et al., 2013; Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Language regions show little or no response to tasks in non-linguistic domains, such as executive functions, math, logic, music, action observation, and non-linguistic communicative signals.
source: However, they show little or no response to tasks in non-linguistic domains, such as executive functions, math, logic, music, action observation, and non-linguistic communicative signals, like gestures (Fedorenko et al., 2011; Jouravlev et al., 2019; Monti et al., 2009; Monti et al., 2012; Pritchett et al., 2018; see Fedorenko and Blank, 2020, for a review).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: If code comprehension relies on the same circuits that map form to meaning in natural language, activity within the language system should be observed.
source: If code comprehension relies on the same circuits that map form to meaning in natural language, we expect to see activity within the language system.
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about the language system and logical inference.

claim: Prior neuroimaging studies have provided some evidence for left-lateralized activity in regions that roughly correspond to the language system during code comprehension.
source: Existing studies have provided some evidence for left-lateralized activity in regions that roughly correspond to the language system (Siegmund et al., 2014; Siegmund et al., 2017), as well as some evidence for the engagement of frontal and parietal regions resembling the MD system (Floyd et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Siegmund et al., 2014; Siegmund et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Prior neuroimaging studies have provided some evidence for the engagement of frontal and parietal regions resembling the MD system during code comprehension.
source: Existing studies have provided some evidence for left-lateralized activity in regions that roughly correspond to the language system (Siegmund et al., 2014; Siegmund et al., 2017), as well as some evidence for the engagement of frontal and parietal regions resembling the MD system (Floyd et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Siegmund et al., 2014; Siegmund et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: None of the prior neuroimaging studies of programming sought to explicitly distinguish code comprehension from other programming-related processes.
source: However, none of these prior studies sought to explicitly distinguish code comprehension from other programming-related processes, and none of them provide quantitative evaluations of putative shared responses to code and other tasks, such as working memory, math, or language (cf. Liu et al., 2020; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research based on review of the literature.

claim: Contrasting neural responses evoked by code problems with those evoked by content-matched sentence problems allows disentangling activity evoked by code comprehension from activity evoked by the underlying program content.
source: First, we contrast neural responses evoked by code problems with those evoked by content-matched sentence problems (Figure 1A); this comparison allows us to disentangle activity evoked by code comprehension from activity evoked by the underlying program content (which is matched across code and sentence problems).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the experimental design, based on logical inference.

claim: The functional localization approach obviates the reliance on 'reverse inference' reasoning.
source: The functional localization approach obviates the reliance on the much-criticized 'reverse inference' reasoning (Poldrack, 2006; Poldrack, 2011), whereby functions are inferred from coarse macro-anatomical landmarks.
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citations to prior methodological critiques.

claim: Localization of the MD and language networks in individual participants is important given substantial variability in their precise locations across individuals.
source: In addition, localization of the MD and language networks is performed in individual participants, which is important given substantial variability in their precise locations across individuals (Fedorenko and Blank, 2020; Shashidhara et al., 2019b) and leads to higher sensitivity and functional resolution (Nieto-Castañón and Fedorenko, 2012).
evidence: This methodological claim is supported by citations to prior research on individual variability.

claim: Individual localization leads to higher sensitivity and functional resolution.
source: In addition, localization of the MD and language networks is performed in individual participants, which is important given substantial variability in their precise locations across individuals (Fedorenko and Blank, 2020; Shashidhara et al., 2019b) and leads to higher sensitivity and functional resolution (Nieto-Castañón and Fedorenko, 2012).
evidence: This methodological claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Python is a popular general-purpose programming language.
source: Python, a popular general-purpose programming language
evidence: This is a factual statement about Python based on established knowledge.

claim: ScratchJr is an introductory visual programming language for creating animations, designed for young children.
source: ScratchJr, an introductory visual programming language for creating animations, designed for young children (Bers and Resnick, 2015)
evidence: This is a factual statement about ScratchJr supported by citation.

claim: Comprehension of both Python and ScratchJr code requires retrieving the meaning of program tokens and combining them into statements.
source: Comprehension of both Python and ScratchJr code requires retrieving the meaning of program tokens and combining them into statements, despite the fact that the visual features of the tokens in the two languages are very different (text vs. images).
evidence: This is a claim about cognitive processes based on knowledge of programming languages.

claim: If a brain system is involved in code comprehension, its response should generalize across programming languages and problem types.
source: If a brain system is involved in code comprehension, we expect its response to generalize across programming languages and problem types, similar to how distinct natural languages in bilinguals and multilinguals draw on the same language regions (Kroll et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction based on prior knowledge about language processing in bilinguals and logical inference.

claim: Distinct natural languages in bilinguals and multilinguals draw on the same language regions.
source: If a brain system is involved in code comprehension, we expect its response to generalize across programming languages and problem types, similar to how distinct natural languages in bilinguals and multilinguals draw on the same language regions (Kroll et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Participants in Experiment 1 achieved 99.6% response rate and 85% accuracy on code problems.
source: Good behavioral performance confirmed that participants were proficient in the relevant programming language and engaged with the task (Python: 99.6% response rate, 85% accuracy on code problems; ScratchJr: 98.6% response rate, 79% accuracy on code problems; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for detailed behavioral results).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data collected in the experiment.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 achieved 98.6% response rate and 79% accuracy on code problems.
source: Good behavioral performance confirmed that participants were proficient in the relevant programming language and engaged with the task (Python: 99.6% response rate, 85% accuracy on code problems; ScratchJr: 98.6% response rate, 79% accuracy on code problems; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for detailed behavioral results).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data collected in the experiment.

claim: Good behavioral performance confirmed that participants were proficient in the relevant programming language and engaged with the task.
source: Good behavioral performance confirmed that participants were proficient in the relevant programming language and engaged with the task (Python: 99.6% response rate, 85% accuracy on code problems; ScratchJr: 98.6% response rate, 79% accuracy on code problems; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for detailed behavioral results).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The MD system exhibited strong bilateral responses to code problems in both Python and ScratchJr experiments.
source: We found strong bilateral responses to code problems within the MD system in both Experiments 1 and 2 (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data presented in the figures.

claim: MD system responses to code problems were stronger than responses to sentence problems in both Python (β = 1.03, p<0.001) and ScratchJr (β = 1.38, p<0.001) experiments.
source: These responses were stronger than responses to both the sentence problem condition (Python: β = 1.03, p<0.001, ScratchJr: β = 1.38, p<0.001) and the control nonword reading condition (Python: β = 2.17, p<0.001; ScratchJr: β = 1.23, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: MD system responses to code problems were stronger than responses to the control nonword reading condition in both Python (β = 2.17, p<0.001) and ScratchJr (β = 1.23, p<0.001) experiments.
source: These responses were stronger than responses to both the sentence problem condition (Python: β = 1.03, p<0.001, ScratchJr: β = 1.38, p<0.001) and the control nonword reading condition (Python: β = 2.17, p<0.001; ScratchJr: β = 1.23, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The fact that code problems drove the MD system more strongly than content-matched sentence problems demonstrates that the MD system responds to code comprehension specifically rather than simply being activated by the underlying problem content.
source: The fact that code problems drove the MD system more strongly than content-matched sentence problems (despite the fact that sentence problems generally took longer to respond to; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1) demonstrates that the MD system responds to code comprehension specifically rather than simply being activated by the underlying problem content.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of fMRI results and behavioral data.

claim: Neither Python nor ScratchJr problems showed a left-hemisphere bias for code comprehension.
source: Neither Python nor ScratchJr problems showed a left-hemisphere bias for code comprehension.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of hemispheric differences in the fMRI data.

claim: For Python, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect did not interact with hemisphere (β = 0.11, p=0.46).
source: For Python, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect did not interact with hemisphere (β = 0.11, p=0.46), even though the magnitude of responses to code problems as compared to nonword reading was stronger in the left hemisphere (β = 0.63, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: For Python, the magnitude of responses to code problems as compared to nonword reading was stronger in the left hemisphere (β = 0.63, p<0.001).
source: For Python, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect did not interact with hemisphere (β = 0.11, p=0.46), even though the magnitude of responses to code problems as compared to nonword reading was stronger in the left hemisphere (β = 0.63, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Neural activity evoked by Python code comprehension was bilaterally distributed but activity evoked by the underlying problem content was left-lateralized.
source: These results show that neural activity evoked by Python code comprehension was bilaterally distributed but that activity evoked by the underlying problem content was left-lateralized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of hemispheric differences in the fMRI data.

claim: For ScratchJr, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect interacted with hemisphere, with stronger responses in the right hemisphere (β = 0.57, p=0.001).
source: For ScratchJr, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect interacted with hemisphere, with stronger responses in the right hemisphere (β = 0.57, p=0.001), perhaps reflecting the bias of the right hemisphere toward visuo-spatial processing (Corballis, 2003; Hugdahl, 2011; Sheremata et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The right hemisphere bias for ScratchJr may reflect the bias of the right hemisphere toward visuo-spatial processing.
source: For ScratchJr, the size of the code problems > sentence problems effect interacted with hemisphere, with stronger responses in the right hemisphere (β = 0.57, p=0.001), perhaps reflecting the bias of the right hemisphere toward visuo-spatial processing (Corballis, 2003; Hugdahl, 2011; Sheremata et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior research on hemispheric specialization.

claim: 17 of the 20 MD fROIs responded significantly more strongly to Python code problems than to sentence problems.
source: Follow-up analyses of activity in individual regions within the MD system demonstrated that 17 of the 20 MD fROIs (all except the fROIs located in left medial frontal cortex and in the left and right insula) responded significantly more strongly to Python code problems than to sentence problems (see Supplementary file 1 for all fROI statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual fROIs.

claim: For ScratchJr, responses were significantly stronger than responses to sentence problems in 6 of the 10 left hemisphere MD fROIs.
source: Responses to ScratchJr were significantly stronger than responses to sentence problems in 6 of the 10 left hemisphere MD fROIs (the effect was not significant in the fROIs in superior frontal gyrus, the dorsal part of the precentral gyrus, the medial frontal cortex, and the insula) and in 8 of the 10 right hemisphere MD fROIs (the effect was not significant in the fROIs in the medial frontal cortex and the insula; see Supplementary file 1 for all fROI statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual fROIs.

claim: For ScratchJr, responses were significantly stronger than responses to sentence problems in 8 of the 10 right hemisphere MD fROIs.
source: Responses to ScratchJr were significantly stronger than responses to sentence problems in 6 of the 10 left hemisphere MD fROIs (the effect was not significant in the fROIs in superior frontal gyrus, the dorsal part of the precentral gyrus, the medial frontal cortex, and the insula) and in 8 of the 10 right hemisphere MD fROIs (the effect was not significant in the fROIs in the medial frontal cortex and the insula; see Supplementary file 1 for all fROI statistics).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of individual fROIs.

claim: Code processing is broadly distributed across the MD system rather than being localized to a particular region or to a small subset of regions.
source: These analyses demonstrate that code processing is broadly distributed across the MD system rather than being localized to a particular region or to a small subset of regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results across individual fROIs.

claim: MD responses to code are strong, do not exclusively reflect responses to problem content, generalize across programming languages and problem types, and are observed across most MD fROIs.
source: Overall, we show that MD responses to code are strong, do not exclusively reflect responses to problem content, generalize across programming languages and problem types, and are observed across most MD fROIs.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the pattern of fMRI results.

claim: Three left frontal fROIs ('precentral_A', 'precentral_B', and 'midFrontal') exhibited stronger responses to Python code problems than to the hard working memory task.
source: Three fROIs located in the left frontal lobe ('precentral_A', 'precentral_B', and 'midFrontal') exhibited stronger responses to Python code problems than to the hard working memory task (β = 1.21, p<0.001; β = 1.89, p<0.001; and β = 0.79, p=0.011, respectively; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The magnitude of the code problems > sentence problems contrast in the three left frontal fROIs was comparable to the average response magnitude across all MD fROIs.
source: However, the magnitude of the code problems > sentence problems contrast in these regions (β = 1.03, 0.95, 0.97) was comparable to the average response magnitude across all MD fROIs (average β = 1.03), suggesting that the high response was caused by processing the underlying problem content rather than by code comprehension per se.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of effect sizes.

claim: No MD fROIs exhibited higher responses to ScratchJr code compared to the hard working memory task.
source: Furthermore, neither these nor any other MD fROIs exhibited higher responses to ScratchJr code compared to the hard working memory task (in fact, the 'precentral_A' fROI did not even show a significant code problems > sentence problems effect).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Code comprehension is broadly supported by the MD system, but no MD regions are functionally specialized to process computer code.
source: We conclude that code comprehension is broadly supported by the MD system (similar to, e.g., intuitive physical inference; Fischer et al., 2016), but no MD regions are functionally specialized to process computer code.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of fMRI results, with comparison to prior research.

claim: The responses to code problems within the language system were weaker than responses to sentence problems in both Python (β = 0.98, p<0.001) and ScratchJr (β = 0.99, p<0.001) experiments.
source: The responses to code problems within the language system (Figures 2 and 3) were weaker than responses to sentence problems in both experiments (Python: β = 0.98, p<0.001; ScratchJr: β = 0.99, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Responses to Python code problems were stronger than the responses to nonword reading (β = 0.78, p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, although the responses to code problems were stronger than the responses to nonword reading for Python (β = 0.78, p<0.001), this was not the case for ScratchJr (β = 0.15, p=0.29), suggesting that the language system is not consistently engaged during computer code comprehension.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Responses to ScratchJr code problems were not stronger than responses to nonword reading (β = 0.15, p=0.29).
source: Furthermore, although the responses to code problems were stronger than the responses to nonword reading for Python (β = 0.78, p<0.001), this was not the case for ScratchJr (β = 0.15, p=0.29), suggesting that the language system is not consistently engaged during computer code comprehension.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The language system is not consistently engaged during computer code comprehension.
source: Furthermore, although the responses to code problems were stronger than the responses to nonword reading for Python (β = 0.78, p<0.001), this was not the case for ScratchJr (β = 0.15, p=0.29), suggesting that the language system is not consistently engaged during computer code comprehension.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of language system responses across the two experiments.

claim: There was no effect of identifier language (English vs. Japanese) on language system responses to Python code (β = 0.03, p=0.84).
source: We found no effect of identifier language (β = 0.03, p=0.84), knowledge of Japanese (β = 0.03, p=0.93), or interaction between them (β = 0.09, p=0.71), indicating that the language system's response to Python code was not driven by the presence of semantically transparent identifiers.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data comparing English and Japanese identifier conditions.

claim: There was no effect of knowledge of Japanese on language system responses to Python code (β = 0.03, p=0.93).
source: We found no effect of identifier language (β = 0.03, p=0.84), knowledge of Japanese (β = 0.03, p=0.93), or interaction between them (β = 0.09, p=0.71), indicating that the language system's response to Python code was not driven by the presence of semantically transparent identifiers.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: There was no interaction between identifier language and knowledge of Japanese on language system responses (β = 0.09, p=0.71).
source: We found no effect of identifier language (β = 0.03, p=0.84), knowledge of Japanese (β = 0.03, p=0.93), or interaction between them (β = 0.09, p=0.71), indicating that the language system's response to Python code was not driven by the presence of semantically transparent identifiers.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The language system's response to Python code was not driven by the presence of semantically transparent identifiers.
source: We found no effect of identifier language (β = 0.03, p=0.84), knowledge of Japanese (β = 0.03, p=0.93), or interaction between them (β = 0.09, p=0.71), indicating that the language system's response to Python code was not driven by the presence of semantically transparent identifiers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis of the identifier manipulation.

claim: The language system shows strong sensitivity to word meanings.
source: This result is somewhat surprising given the language system's strong sensitivity to word meanings (e.g., Anderson et al., 2019; Binder et al., 2009; Fedorenko et al., 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2020; Pereira et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Activation patterns were highly correlated between code and sentence problems in the language system (r = 0.69, p<0.001).
source: We found that the activation patterns were highly correlated between the code and sentence problems (r = 0.69, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by spatial correlation analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Correlation values between code and sentence problems were higher than the correlations between code problems and sentence reading (0.69 vs. 0.65; p<0.001).
source: These correlation values were higher than the correlations between code problems and sentence reading (0.69 vs. 0.65; p<0.001), although lower than the correlations within the code problem condition (0.69 vs. 0.73; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of spatial correlations.

claim: Correlation values between code and sentence problems were lower than the correlations within the code problem condition (0.69 vs. 0.73; p<0.001).
source: These correlation values were higher than the correlations between code problems and sentence reading (0.69 vs. 0.65; p<0.001), although lower than the correlations within the code problem condition (0.69 vs. 0.73; p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of spatial correlations.

claim: The language system is sensitive to the content of the stimulus rather than just the stimulus type (code vs. words).
source: The fact that code and sentence problem responses are correlated over and above code problem and sentence reading responses indicates that the language system is sensitive to the content of the stimulus rather than just the stimulus type (code vs. words).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of spatial correlations.

claim: Problem content can account for a substantial portion of the response in the language regions (Δr = 0.04).
source: Moreover, similar to the MD system, problem content can account for a substantial portion of the response in the language regions (Δr = 0.04).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of spatial correlations.

claim: In both MD and language systems, response to Python code is driven both by problem content and by code-specific responses.
source: Thus, in both MD and language systems, response to Python code is driven both by problem content and by code-specific responses.
evidence: This is a summary inference drawn from the spatial correlation analyses.

claim: The language system responded to code problems written in Python but not in ScratchJr.
source: Overall, we found that the language system responded to code problems written in Python but not in ScratchJr.
evidence: This is a summary of the pattern of language system responses across experiments.

claim: Python responses in the language system were driven not only by code comprehension, but also by the processing of problem content.
source: Furthermore, Python responses were driven not only by code comprehension, but also by the processing of problem content.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial correlation analysis.

claim: Successful comprehension of computer code can proceed without engaging the language network.
source: We conclude that successful comprehension of computer code can proceed without engaging the language network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of language system responses, particularly the lack of response to ScratchJr.

claim: In both Python and ScratchJr experiments, the discovered regions from whole-brain analysis spatially resembled the MD system.
source: In both experiments, the discovered regions spatially resembled the MD system (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is based on whole-brain GSS analysis results.

claim: For Python, any region that responded to code also responded to the spatial working memory task.
source: For Python, any region that responded to code also responded to the spatial working memory task (the MD localizer).
evidence: This claim is based on whole-brain analysis examining responses across conditions.

claim: For ScratchJr, some fROIs responded more strongly to code problems than to the spatial working memory task and were located in early visual areas/ventral visual stream.
source: In case of ScratchJr, some fROIs responded more strongly to code problems than to the spatial working memory task; these fROIs were located in early visual areas/ventral visual stream and therefore likely responded to low-level visual properties of ScratchJr code (which includes colorful icons, objects, etc.).
evidence: This claim is based on whole-brain analysis and anatomical localization of responsive regions.

claim: Visual fROIs that responded to ScratchJr likely responded to low-level visual properties of ScratchJr code.
source: In case of ScratchJr, some fROIs responded more strongly to code problems than to the spatial working memory task; these fROIs were located in early visual areas/ventral visual stream and therefore likely responded to low-level visual properties of ScratchJr code (which includes colorful icons, objects, etc.).
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of the responsive regions and the visual properties of ScratchJr.

claim: The MD system responds robustly and consistently to computer code.
source: These whole-brain analyses demonstrate that the MD system responds robustly and consistently to computer code, recapitulating the results of the fROI-based analyses (Figures 2–4), and show that fROI-based analyses did not miss any non-visual code-responsive or code-selective regions outside the boundaries of the MD system.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on convergence of whole-brain and fROI-based analyses.

claim: fROI-based analyses did not miss any non-visual code-responsive or code-selective regions outside the boundaries of the MD system.
source: These whole-brain analyses demonstrate that the MD system responds robustly and consistently to computer code, recapitulating the results of the fROI-based analyses (Figures 2–4), and show that fROI-based analyses did not miss any non-visual code-responsive or code-selective regions outside the boundaries of the MD system.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of whole-brain and fROI-based analysis results.

claim: No correlations between proficiency and MD/language system responses were significant.
source: We correlated responses within each system with independently obtained proficiency scores for Experiment 1 participants (see the paper's website for details: https://github.com/ALFA-group/neural-program-comprehension; Ivanova and Srikant, 2020; copy archived at swh:1:rev:616e893d05038da620bdf9f2964bd3befba75dc5) and with in-scanner accuracy scores for Experiment 2 participants. No correlations were significant (see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis of proficiency measures with brain responses.

claim: Strong responses to code problems were observed in the MD system regardless of problem type (math vs. string manipulation).
source: Strong responses were observed in the MD system (Figure 4A and B) regardless of problem type (β = 3.02, p<0.001; no difference between problem types) and problem structure (β = 3.14, p<0.001; sequential problems evoked a slightly weaker response, β = −0.20, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data across problem types.

claim: Strong responses to code problems were observed in the MD system regardless of problem structure (sequential, for loops, if statements).
source: Strong responses were observed in the MD system (Figure 4A and B) regardless of problem type (β = 3.02, p<0.001; no difference between problem types) and problem structure (β = 3.14, p<0.001; sequential problems evoked a slightly weaker response, β = −0.20, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data across problem structures.

claim: Sequential problems evoked a slightly weaker response in the MD system (β = −0.20, p=0.002).
source: Strong responses were observed in the MD system (Figure 4A and B) regardless of problem type (β = 3.02, p<0.001; no difference between problem types) and problem structure (β = 3.14, p<0.001; sequential problems evoked a slightly weaker response, β = −0.20, p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: The responses in the MD system were not driven by one particular type of problem or by mental operations related to the processing of a particular code structure.
source: This analysis demonstrates that the responses were not driven by one particular type of problem or by mental operations related to the processing of a particular code structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of strong differences across problem types and structures.

claim: Earlier reports of left-lateralized code-evoked activity may reflect processing program content rather than code comprehension per se.
source: Our findings suggest that earlier reports of left-lateralized code-evoked activity (Siegmund et al., 2014) may reflect processing program content rather than code comprehension per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current study's findings about lateralization, compared to prior research.

claim: The results align well with the results of another recent study on program comprehension by Liu et al., 2020.
source: The results of our work align well with the results of another recent study on program comprehension (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research.

claim: Liu et al. investigated the neural correlates of program comprehension by contrasting Python code problems with fake code.
source: Liu et al. investigated the neural correlates of program comprehension by contrasting Python code problems with fake code.
evidence: This is a description of prior research.

claim: The code problems > fake code contrast in Liu et al. is broader than the current study's contrast because it includes both code comprehension and the processing of problem content.
source: The code problem condition was similar to ours, whereas the fake code condition involved viewing scrambled code, followed by a visual recognition task. The code problems > fake code contrast is broader than ours: it includes both code comprehension (interpreting Python code) and the processing of problem content (manipulating characters in a string).
evidence: This is a comparison and interpretation of methodological differences between studies.

claim: The MD system is involved in both code comprehension and processing of problem content.
source: Our results show that the MD system is involved in both processes, but Python code comprehension is bilateral, whereas the processing of problem content is left-lateralized.
evidence: This is a summary of the current study's findings.

claim: Python code comprehension is bilateral, whereas the processing of problem content is left-lateralized.
source: Our results show that the MD system is involved in both processes, but Python code comprehension is bilateral, whereas the processing of problem content is left-lateralized.
evidence: This is a summary of the lateralization findings from the current study.

claim: Liu et al. conclude that it is the MD regions, not the language regions, that are primarily involved in program comprehension.
source: Further, similar to us, Liu et al. conclude that it is the MD regions, not the language regions, that are primarily involved in program comprehension.
evidence: This is a description of conclusions from prior research.

claim: The MD system's engagement in code comprehension reflects the use of domain-general executive processes.
source: The fact that the MD system responds to code problems over and above content-matched sentence problems underscores the role of domain-general executive processes in code comprehension.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current study's findings.

claim: Code comprehension elicits bilateral responses within the MD system, in contrast to math and logic tasks that tend to elicit left-lateralized responses.
source: In particular, code comprehension elicits bilateral responses within the MD system, in contrast to math and logic tasks that tend to elicit left-lateralized responses within the MD system, and in contrast to language tasks that elicit responses in the spatially and functionally distinct language system.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with prior knowledge about other cognitive domains.

claim: Responses in the MD system were driven both by the processing of problem content and by code comprehension.
source: We found that responses in the MD system were driven both by the processing of problem content (e.g., summing the contents of an array) and by code comprehension (e.g., identifying variables referring to an array and its elements, interpreting a for loop, realizing that the output of the program is the variable being updated inside the for loop).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of MD system responses.

claim: Both processing problem content and code comprehension plausibly require attention, working memory, inhibitory control, planning, and general flexible relational reasoning.
source: Both of these processes plausibly require attention, working memory, inhibitory control, planning, and general flexible relational reasoning – cognitive processes long linked to the MD system (Duncan, 2010; Duncan, 2013; Duncan and Owen, 2000; Miller and Cohen, 2001) in both humans (Assem et al., 2020; Shashidhara et al., 2019a; Woolgar et al., 2018) and non-human primates (Freedman et al., 2001; Miller et al., 1996; Mitchell et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference about cognitive processes based on prior research on the MD system.

claim: Huang et al., 2019 reported neural overlap between operations on programming data structures and a mental rotation task within brain regions whose topography resembles the MD system.
source: A recent study (Huang et al., 2019) reported neural overlap between operations on programming data structures (which require both code comprehension and the processing of problem content) and a mental rotation task (which requires spatial reasoning). The overlap was observed within brain regions whose topography grossly resembles that of the MD system.
evidence: This is a description of findings from prior research.

claim: In the current study, all code-responsive brain regions outside the visual cortex also responded robustly during a spatial memory task.
source: In our study, all code-responsive brain regions outside the visual cortex also responded robustly during a spatial memory task (Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4), similar to the results reported in Huang et al., 2019.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of responses across tasks in the current study.

claim: The MD system is not specifically tuned to spatial reasoning.
source: However, the MD system is not specifically tuned to spatial reasoning (Duncan, 2010; Fedorenko et al., 2013; Michalka et al., 2015), so the overlap between code comprehension and spatial reasoning likely reflects the engagement of domain-general cognitive processes, like working memory and cognitive control, as opposed to processes specific to spatial reasoning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents an interpretation of the overlap findings.

claim: Code-specific knowledge representations are stored within the MD system.
source: Furthermore, given that no regions outside of the MD system showed code-specific responses, it must be the case that code-specific knowledge representations are also stored within this system (see Hasson et al., 2015, for a general discussion of the lack of distinction between storage and computing resources in the brain).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results, supported by citation to theoretical work.

claim: Code-specific representations would likely include both knowledge specific to a programming language and knowledge of programming concepts that are shared across languages.
source: Such code-specific representations would likely include both knowledge specific to a programming language (e.g., the syntax marking an array in Java vs. Python) and knowledge of programming concepts that are shared across languages (e.g., for loops).
evidence: This is a speculation about the nature of code representations based on knowledge of programming.

claim: The MD system can flexibly store task-relevant information in the short term.
source: Much evidence suggests that the MD system can flexibly store task-relevant information in the short term (e.g., Fedorenko et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2001; Shashidhara et al., 2019a; Wen et al., 2019; Woolgar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The MD system can store some domain-specific representations in the long term, perhaps for evolutionarily late-emerging and ontogenetically late-acquired domains of knowledge.
source: However, evidence from studies on processing mathematics (e.g., Amalric and Dehaene, 2019) and physics (e.g., Cetron et al., 2019; Fischer et al., 2016) further suggests that the MD system can store some domain-specific representations in the long term, perhaps for evolutionarily late-emerging and ontogenetically late-acquired domains of knowledge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on mathematics and physics processing.

claim: The current data add to evidence that the MD system stores and uses information required for code comprehension.
source: Our data add to this body of evidence by showing that the MD system stores and uses information required for code comprehension.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of prior research.

claim: Code-evoked responses are distributed throughout the MD system instead of being concentrated in one region or a subset.
source: We also show that, instead of being concentrated in one region or a subset of the MD system, code-evoked responses are distributed throughout the MD system.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial distribution findings from the fROI analyses.

claim: Selectivity for code comprehension in a subset of the MD network may only emerge with years of experience in professional programmers.
source: First, selectivity for code comprehension in a subset of the MD network may only emerge with years of experience (e.g., in professional programmers). Participants in our experiments were all proficient in the target programming language but most had only a few years of experience with it.
evidence: This is a speculation about how expertise might affect neural organization.

claim: Code-selective subsets of the MD network may be detectable at higher spatial resolution, using invasive methods like electrocorticography or single-cell recordings.
source: Second, code-selective subsets of the MD network may be detectable at higher spatial resolution, using invasive methods like electrocorticography (Parvizi and Kastner, 2018) or single-cell recordings (Mukamel and Fried, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about methodological limitations, supported by citations to invasive methods.

claim: The need to flexibly solve novel problems throughout one's life may prevent the 'crystallization' of specialized subnetworks within the MD cortex.
source: And third, perhaps the need to flexibly solve novel problems throughout one's life prevents the 'crystallization' of specialized subnetworks within the MD cortex.
evidence: This is a speculation about functional organization principles.

claim: Some subset of the MD network may be causally important for code comprehension even though it does not show strong selectivity for it.
source: All that said, it may also be the case that some subset of the MD network is causally important for code comprehension even though it does not show strong selectivity for it, similar to how damage to some MD areas (mostly, in the left parietal cortex) appears to lead to deficits in numerical cognition (Ardila and Rosselli, 2002; Kahn and Whitaker, 1991; Lemer et al., 2003; Rosselli and Ardila, 1989; Takayama et al., 1994), even though these regions do not show selectivity for numerical tasks in fMRI (Pinel et al., 2004; Shuman and Kanwisher, 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by analogy to findings from numerical cognition research.

claim: The language system does not respond consistently during code comprehension in spite of numerous similarities between code and natural languages.
source: We found that the language system does not respond consistently during code comprehension in spite of numerous similarities between code and natural languages (Fedorenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of the language system findings from the current study.

claim: Some accounts of language processing claim that syntactic operations are highly abstract and insensitive to the nature of the to-be-combined units.
source: Some accounts of language processing claim that syntactic operations that support language processing are highly abstract and insensitive to the nature of the to-be-combined units (e.g., Berwick et al., 2013; Fitch et al., 2005; Fitch and Martins, 2014; Hauser et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of theoretical accounts from prior research.

claim: Accounts claiming abstract syntactic operations predict that mechanisms supporting structure processing in language should also get engaged when processing structure in other domains, including computer code.
source: Such accounts predict that the mechanisms supporting structure processing in language should also get engaged when we process structure in other domains, including computer code.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from theoretical accounts.

claim: Processing music does not engage the language system.
source: Prior work has already put into question this idea in its broadest form: processing music, whose hierarchical structure has long been noted to have parallels with linguistic syntax (e.g., Lerdahl and Jackendoff, 1996; cf. Jackendoff, 2009), does not engage the language system (e.g., Fedorenko et al., 2011; Rogalsky et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on music and language.

claim: The current finding shows that compositional input and hierarchical structure do not necessarily engage language-specific regions.
source: Our finding builds upon the results from the music domain to show that compositional input (here, variables and keywords combining into statements) and hierarchical structure (here, conditional statements and loops) do not necessarily engage language-specific regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of prior research on music.

claim: Studies of math and logic show that those domains do not rely on the language system.
source: Studies of math and logic, domains that also make extensive use of symbols, show that those domains do not rely on the language system (Amalric and Dehaene, 2019; Cohen et al., 2000; Fedorenko et al., 2011; Monti et al., 2009; Monti et al., 2012; Pinel and Dehaene, 2010; Varley et al., 2005), a conclusion consistent with our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on math and logic.

claim: The computer code problems designed in this study are not only symbolic, but also refer to the same conceptual representations as the corresponding verbal problems.
source: Our work provides an even stronger test of the symbolic reference hypothesis: the computer code problems we designed are not only symbolic, but also refer to the same conceptual representations as the corresponding verbal problems (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a claim about the experimental design and its implications.

claim: Each ScratchJr code problem refers to a sequence of actions performed by a cartoon character, which is a clear case of reference to concepts in the physical world.
source: This parallel is particularly striking in the case of ScratchJr: each code problem refers to a sequence of actions performed by a cartoon character – a clear case of reference to concepts in the physical world.
evidence: This is a description of the ScratchJr stimuli and their semantic properties.

claim: The language regions do not respond to ScratchJr, showing a clear preference for language over other types of meaningful structured input.
source: And yet, the language regions do not respond to ScratchJr, showing a clear preference for language over other types of meaningful structured input (see also Ivanova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ScratchJr findings, supported by citation to related work.

claim: Python and ScratchJr are very high-level programming languages that emphasize human readability over computational efficiency.
source: The programming languages we chose are very high- level, meaning that they emphasize human readability (Buse and Weimer, 2010; Klare, 1963) over computational efficiency.
evidence: This is a claim about the properties of the programming languages used, supported by citations.

claim: ScratchJr is optimized to be accessible and engaging for young children.
source: ScratchJr is further optimized to be accessible and engaging for young children (Sullivan and Bers, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work on ScratchJr.

claim: Code written in Python and ScratchJr is meant to be read and understood by humans, not just executed by machines.
source: Thus, code written in these languages is meant to be read and understood by humans, not just executed by machines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of high-level programming languages.

claim: Computer code comprehension is similar to reading in natural language in that the goal is to extract a meaningful message produced by another human.
source: In this respect, computer code comprehension is similar to reading in natural language: the goal is to extract a meaningful message produced by another human at some point in the past.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the communicative properties of code and language.

claim: The communicative nature of code comprehension is not sufficient to recruit the language system.
source: And yet the communicative nature of this activity is not sufficient to recruit the language system, consistent with previous reports showing a neural dissociation between language and other communication-related activities, such as gesture processing (Jouravlev et al., 2019), intentional actions (Pritchett et al., 2018), or theory of mind tasks (Apperly et al., 2006; Dronkers et al., 1998; Jacoby et al., 2016; Paunov et al., 2019; Varley and Siegal, 2000).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior research on communication and language.

claim: The lack of consistent language system engagement in code comprehension does not mean that the mechanisms underlying language and code processing are completely different.
source: Of course, the lack of consistent language system engagement in code comprehension does not mean that the mechanisms underlying language and code processing are completely different.
evidence: This is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: It is possible that both language and MD regions have similarly organized neural circuits that allow them to process combinatorial input or map between a symbol and the concept it refers to.
source: It is possible that both language and MD regions have similarly organized neural circuits that allow them to process combinatorial input or map between a symbol and the concept it refers to.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential similarities in neural mechanisms.

claim: Code comprehension does not load on the same neural circuits as language and needs to use domain-general MD circuits instead.
source: However, the fact that we observed code-evoked activity primarily in the MD regions indicates that code comprehension does not load on the same neural circuits as language and needs to use domain-general MD circuits instead.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pattern of results.

claim: The language system may play a role in learning to program, even if it is not required to support code comprehension once the skill is learned.
source: Finally, it is possible that the language system may play a role in learning to program (Prat et al., 2020), even if it is not required to support code comprehension once the skill is learned.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Studies advocating the 'coding as another language' approach have found that treating coding as a meaning-making activity had a positive impact on teaching and learning to program.
source: Studies advocating the 'coding as another language' approach (Bers, 2019; Bers, 2018; Sullivan and Bers, 2019) have found that treating coding as a meaning-making activity rather than merely a problem-solving skill had a positive impact on both teaching and learning to program in the classroom (Hassenfeld et al., 2020; Hassenfeld and Bers, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior educational research.

claim: The language system and/or the general semantic system might play a role in learning to process computer code, especially in children.
source: Such results indicate that the language system and/or the general semantic system might play a role in learning to process computer code, especially in children, when the language system is still developing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on educational findings and developmental considerations.

claim: The stimuli used in the study were short and only included a few basic elements of control flow.
source: The stimuli used in our study were short and only included a few basic elements of control flow (such as for loops and if statements).
evidence: This is a description of the study's limitations.

claim: The study focused on code comprehension, which is a necessary but not sufficient component of many other programming activities.
source: Furthermore, we focused on code comprehension, which is a necessary but not sufficient component of many other programming activities, such as code generation, editing, and debugging.
evidence: This is a description of the study's scope and limitations.

claim: Reading more complex pieces of code might recruit an extended, or a different, set of brain regions, similar to how narrative processing recruits systems outside the regions that support single sentence processing.
source: Just like narrative processing recruits systems outside the regions that support single sentence processing (Baldassano et al., 2018; Blank and Fedorenko, 2020; Ferstl et al., 2008; Jacoby and Fedorenko, 2020; Lerner et al., 2011; Simony et al., 2016), reading more complex pieces of code might recruit an extended, or a different, set of brain regions.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions, supported by analogy to language processing research.

claim: Investigations of expert programmers may reveal changes in how programming knowledge and use are instantiated in the mind and brain as a function of increasing domain-relevant experience.
source: Furthermore, as noted above, investigations of expert programmers may reveal changes in how programming knowledge and use are instantiated in the mind and brain as a function of increasing amount of domain-relevant experience.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Code comprehension consistently recruits the MD system but does not consistently engage the language system.
source: Overall, we provide evidence that code comprehension consistently recruits the MD system – which subserves cognitive processing across multiple cognitive domains – but does not consistently engage the language system, in spite of numerous similarities between natural and programming languages.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: By isolating neural activity specific to code comprehension, the study paves the way for future studies examining the cognitive and neural correlates of programming.
source: By isolating neural activity specific to code comprehension, we pave the way for future studies examining the cognitive and neural correlates of programming and contribute to the broader literature on the neural systems that support novel cognitive tools.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution and implications of the study.

claim: For Experiment 1, 25 participants were recruited, with 15 women and mean age of 23.0 years (SD = 3.0).
source: For Experiment 1, we recruited 25 participants (15 women, mean age = 23.0 years, SD = 3.0).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The average age at which Experiment 1 participants started to program was 16 years (SD = 2.6).
source: Average age at which participants started to program was 16 years (SD = 2.6); average number of years spent programming was 6.3 (SD = 3.8).
evidence: This is a description of participant programming experience.

claim: The average number of years Experiment 1 participants spent programming was 6.3 (SD = 3.8).
source: Average age at which participants started to program was 16 years (SD = 2.6); average number of years spent programming was 6.3 (SD = 3.8).
evidence: This is a description of participant programming experience.

claim: One left-handed participant had a right-lateralized language system and was excluded from the analyses.
source: Twenty-three participants were right-handed, one was ambidextrous, and one was left-handed (as assessed by Oldfield's [1971] handedness questionnaire); the left-handed participant had a right-lateralized language system and was excluded from the analyses, leaving 24 participants (all of whom had left-lateralized language regions, as evaluated with the language localizer task [see below]).
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusion criteria and final sample.

claim: For Experiment 2, 21 participants were recruited, with 13 women and mean age of 22.5 years (SD = 2.8).
source: For Experiment 2, we recruited 21 participants (13 women, mean age = 22.5 years, SD = 2.8).
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: Two participants from Experiment 2 had to be excluded due to excessive motion during the MRI scan, leaving 19 participants.
source: Two participants from Experiment 2 had to be excluded due to excessive motion during the MRI scan, leaving 19 participants.
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusion and final sample.

claim: All participants were native speakers of English, had normal or corrected to normal vision, and reported working knowledge of Python or ScratchJr.
source: All participants were recruited from MIT, Tufts University, and the surrounding community and paid for participation. All were native speakers of English, had normal or corrected to normal vision, and reported working knowledge of Python or ScratchJr, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: The protocol for the study was approved by MIT's Committee on the Use of Humans as Experimental Subjects (COUHES).
source: The protocol for the study was approved by MIT's Committee on the Use of Humans as Experimental Subjects (COUHES).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: All participants gave written informed consent in accordance with protocol requirements.
source: All participants gave written informed consent in accordance with protocol requirements.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: The program comprehension task in Experiment 1 included three conditions: programs in Python with English identifiers, programs in Python with Japanese identifiers, and sentence versions of those programs.
source: The program comprehension task in Experiment 1 included three conditions: programs in Python with English identifiers, programs in Python with Japanese identifiers, and sentence versions of those programs (visually presented).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each Experiment 1 participant saw 72 problems, and any given participant saw only one version of a problem.
source: Each participant saw 72 problems, and any given participant saw only one version of a problem.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Half of the Experiment 1 problems required performing mathematical operations, and the other half required string manipulations.
source: Half of the problems required performing mathematical operations, and the other half required string manipulations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 1, 1/3 of the problems of each type included only sequential statements, 1/3 included a for loop, and 1/3 included an if statement.
source: In addition, both math and string-manipulation problems varied in program structure: 1/3 of the problems of each type included only sequential statements, 1/3 included a for loop, and 1/3 included an if statement.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The program comprehension task in Experiment 2 included two conditions: short programs in ScratchJr and the sentence versions of those programs.
source: The program comprehension task in Experiment 2 included two conditions: short programs in ScratchJr and the sentence versions of those programs (visually presented).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Each Experiment 2 participant saw 24 problems, and any given participant saw only one version of a problem.
source: Each participant saw 24 problems, and any given participant saw only one version of a problem.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Experiment 2 problems varied in the complexity of the code snippet with three levels of difficulty and eight problems at each level.
source: Furthermore, problems varied in the complexity of the code snippet (three levels of difficulty; eight problems at each level).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The hard > easy contrast in the spatial working memory task has been previously shown to reliably activate bilateral frontal and parietal MD regions.
source: The hard >easy contrast has been previously shown to reliably activate bilateral frontal and parietal MD regions (Assem et al., 2020; Blank et al., 2014; Fedorenko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The same brain regions activated by the hard > easy working memory contrast are activated by diverse executively demanding tasks.
source: Numerous studies have shown that the same brain regions are activated by diverse executively demanding tasks (Duncan and Owen, 2000; Fedorenko et al., 2013; Hugdahl et al., 2015; Shashidhara et al., 2019a; Woolgar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The sentences > nonword lists contrast isolates processes related to language comprehension.
source: The sentences > nonword lists contrast isolates processes related to language comprehension (responses evoked by, e.g., visual perception and reading are subtracted out) and has been previously shown to reliably activate left-lateralized fronto-temporal language processing regions, be robust to changes in task and materials, and activate the same regions regardless of whether the materials were presented visually or auditorily (Fedorenko et al., 2010; Mahowald and Fedorenko, 2016; Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the language localizer.

claim: A similar language network emerges from task-free resting-state data.
source: Further, a similar network emerges from task-free resting-state data (Braga et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Structural and functional data were collected on a 3 Tesla Siemens Trio scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Structural and functional data were collected on the whole-body, 3 Tesla, Siemens Trio scanner with a 32-channel head coil, at the Athinoula A. Martinos Imaging Center at the McGovern Institute for Brain Research at MIT.
evidence: This is a description of the data acquisition methods.

claim: The MD system and the language system are each strongly functionally interconnected.
source: Given the abundant evidence that the MD system and the language system are each strongly functionally interconnected (Blank et al., 2014; Mineroff et al., 2018; Paunov et al., 2019), we perform the key analyses at the system level.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on functional connectivity.
